title: The crow and the rising water
hook: The crows made four clever choices. Two experiments exposed the limits.
paper_title: Using the Aesop's Fable Paradigm to Investigate Causal Understanding of Water Displacement by New Caledonian Crows
citation: Jelbert, Taylor, Cheke, Clayton & Gray (2014), PLOS ONE 9(3):e92895
summary: Six trained New Caledonian crows preferentially selected several functional properties of water displacement, but failed to favor the more efficient narrow tube or a concealed connected U-tube.
evidence_note: Six trained birds began; four completed all six tasks. Narrow-tube first-choice and U-tube performance did not exceed chance, and fixed task order limits causal inference.

evidence.design: Six temporarily captive wild-caught New Caledonian crows; extensive stone-drop training; six tasks with fixed order, 20 trials each; n=6 initially, 5 on tasks 3–4, n=4 on tasks 5–6.

claims.claim: Six trained New Caledonian crows entered the displacement study; only four completed all six experiments.
claims.location: Methods > Subjects, Initial Training; Results opening, cached article lines 50–56 and 74–76.

claims.claim: Most stone drops went into water rather than sand across the first task (76.3%).
claims.location: Methods and Results > Experiment 1, cached article lines 62–63 and 77–78.

claims.claim: Crows selected sinking objects (88.0%) and solid rather than hollow objects (89.0%).
claims.location: Methods and Results > Experiments 2–3, cached article lines 64–67 and 82–85.

claims.claim: The high starting water tube was chosen more often overall (86.8%), with a preference that developed during trials.
claims.location: Methods and Results > Experiment 5, cached article lines 70–71 and 91–92.

claims.claim: No reliable first-drop preference for narrower tubes (56%, p=0.27), and connected U-tube choices near chance (48.9%, p=0.79).
claims.location: Results > Experiments 4 and 6; Discussion, cached article lines 86–94 and 99–103.

limitations: Trained stone dropping, not spontaneous wild water-tool use.
Only four crows completed all six experiments; two stopped because of reduced motivation.
Fixed task order leaves possible learning carryover.
Narrow task produced reachable rewards from either tube, so preference for the efficient one may have been weakly rewarded.
U-tube connection concealed; chance results do not establish species-wide failure of causal reasoning.
No individual-record claims or experimental footage drawn from uninspected Data S1 or Movie S1.
CC0 wild crow reference photo is not from laboratory trials.

editorial_story.audience: Adults curious about wild birds, tool use and physical reasoning; no prior animal cognition training required.
editorial_story.subject: Six trained New Caledonian crows choosing objects and tubes to raise a floating meat reward.
editorial_story.setting: Temporary captivity and controlled six-task testing cage on Grande-Terre, New Caledonia.
editorial_story.opening_context: A clear photo of the actual species, then a conceptual moving water tube with a floating reward out of reach.
editorial_story.normal_expectation: Stones can raise the water, but choosing the objects and tubes that work is a separate challenge.
editorial_story.story_selection: Lead with the concrete obstacle; repeat physical contrasts before the counterexample of a narrow tube and concealed U-tube; close on bounded interpretation.
editorial_story.decisive_limit: Six animals with training and fixed task order, only four completing all tests, no proof of wild discovery or universal understanding.
editorial_story.question: Could trained crows distinguish functional properties of water displacement, including hidden causes?
editorial_story.why_it_matters: Separates useful flexible animal choices from overly broad claims that a species understands all unseen physics.
editorial_story.narrative_arc: Floating food obstacle; initial training; functional water and object choices; higher starting water; first-choice narrow-tube failure; hidden U-tube at chance; training and sample limits; measured conclusion.
editorial_story.closing_payoff: Tested birds selected several useful properties, yet did not consistently discriminate narrow efficiency or concealed connection; intelligence is not a binary score.

posts.caption:
Could a trained crow raise a floating reward with stones? Six New Caledonian crows made choices between materials and water-filled tubes. They more often used water than sand, sinking rather than floating objects, and solid rather than hollow ones. They favoured higher starting water—but did not reliably prefer the more efficient narrow tube or identify a concealed functional U-tube connection. Only four birds completed every test. These controlled tasks show selectivity, not a proof of complete causal understanding or of wild stone-dropping.

Jelbert et al. (2014), PLOS ONE. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0092895
Full open-access paper: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3966847/
Evidence, limitations and credits: https://akshaymohan16.github.io/toxic-tales-library/sources/tt-010.html

Wild crow reference photo: benkeen / iNaturalist, CC0 1.0 (NOT experiment footage). Original water/tube animations are conceptual schematics, not recorded experiments or measured trajectories. Synthetic neural narration, captions and real Toxic Tales logo.

cold_viewer.finding: The organism is immediately identified with a separately licensed wild-specimen photo, followed by a visibly unreachable reward and a simple water-displacement demonstration; no viewer needs to know the Aesop's-fable paradigm.
cold_viewer.basis: First two narrated beats and shot sequence; source species/photo provenance, original Methods apparatus and source-checked physical relationship.

story.finding: The previous producer's original eight narrative beats move from the crow's food obstacle to successful functional contrasts, then two clear failures and the sample limitation; each beat contributes a nonrepetitive scene.
story.basis: Eight spoken segments preserved from earlier source storyboard, first six experiments in main Methods/Results; the narrow and U-tube failures provide a genuine counterturn.

visuals.finding: Source-specific tube/stone diagrams illustrate the water-level mechanism, sand comparison, object density/solidity, starting level and concealed U-tube. The opening and ending species photo is visibly framed as a reference; none of the drawings claim to reproduce laboratory recording or measured time series. Frame/crop/phone-scale compliance remains for independent encoded QA.
visuals.basis: Planned nine new corvus scene families, fixed captions, CC0 benkeen image hash and no reused frog/bee/spider diagrams; pre-render plan only, not video playback.

payoff.finding: The successful choices and failed efficiency/concealed-link decisions reconcile a tempting but exaggerated crows-are-geniuses framing into the scientifically supported conclusion that performance varied with the available property.
payoff.basis: Jelbert et al. Results Experiments 1–6 and Discussion, especially comparison of narrow and connected tube conditions.

scope.finding: The script says six trained New Caledonian crows and finishes with limits to generalizing hidden causation or wild solving. It omits human intelligence-age equivalence and any subjective experience or spontaneous tool invention.
scope.basis: Main article Subject/Initial Training, Results and fixed task order in Discussion. Supplemental Data S1 and footage are not required or used.

retelling.finding: After training, a few crows usually selected items that would lift a floating reward but did not prefer more efficient narrow tubes or infer an unseen connection; small sample and lab training restrict generalization.
retelling.basis: Original eight narration beats, n=6 declining to n=4 and contrasted experiment statistics in main peer-reviewed paper.
